title: Taiwan Moves to Criminalize AI Chip Smuggling to China Under Trade Act
seoTitle: Taiwan Criminalizes AI Chip Smuggling to China
description: Taiwan is amending its Foreign Trade Act to criminalize advanced AI chip and server smuggling to China, introducing prison terms of up to five years.
dek: Taipei plans to close legal loopholes by adding advanced semiconductors and AI servers to its export control list, backing United States restrictions.
keyTakeaways: Taiwan plans to add advanced artificial intelligence chips and AI servers to its controlled export list, making unauthorized shipments to China a criminal offense.
Offenders could face up to five years in prison and fines of approximately $92,500 under the Foreign Trade Act.
The regulatory shift transitions Taiwan from a targeted company blacklist to comprehensive restrictions covering the entire Chinese market.
The policy aligns local enforcement with the United States following the Taiwan-U.S. Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed in January 2026.
body:
The government of Taiwan is preparing legislative changes to criminalize the illicit shipment of advanced artificial intelligence hardware to China. Economic Affairs Minister Kung Ming-hsin confirmed in an interview with Bloomberg that Taipei will formally add high-end semiconductors and AI servers to its strategic export control list. Once enacted, unauthorized shipments will be prosecuted under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act, exposing violators to criminal penalties including prison time.

Under current Taiwanese statutes, unauthorized shipments of advanced computing hardware have largely fallen into legal gray areas, frequently treated merely as administrative violations. By amending export classifications to explicitly cover cutting-edge processors and assembled server racks, authorities aim to give law enforcement direct statutory power to halt unauthorized technology transfers across the Taiwan Strait.

[[FIG1]]

## Closing the Legal Gap in Export Enforcement

Historically, Taiwan's export enforcement framework relied primarily on targeted company blacklists. Authorities added Chinese technology entities such as Huawei and Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC) to the list of strategic high-tech goods in mid-2025, requiring companies to obtain specialized permits before shipping products to those specific firms. However, as reported by [Trending Topics](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/taiwan-wants-to-make-a-i-chip-smuggling-to-china-a-crime/), buyers in China not explicitly blacklisted could still legally receive shipments provided the components did not breach earlier United States export thresholds.

That piecemeal approach left prosecutors with limited tools when uncovering illicit trade routes. According to [Taiwan News](https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/news/6459737), when prosecutors indicted nine individuals in August 2026 over an alleged operation that diverted 130 AI servers—with 74 units allegedly routed to China through third countries using falsified paper trails—investigators had to file charges under general criminal provisions such as document forgery and breach of trust. Existing export control laws lacked explicit criminal offenses tailored to diverted computing equipment.

To address this limitation, Democratic Progressive Party lawmaker Chung Chia-pin has drafted a legislative amendment to the Foreign Trade Act that incorporates a dedicated semiconductor clause targeting unauthorized exports to mainland China. As reported by [Tom's Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/semiconductors/taiwan-targets-illicit-ai-server-exports-to-china-with-five-year-prison-terms-strict-new-controls-follow-us-tariff-deal-and-super-micro-raid), violators caught smuggling controlled computing items under the revised framework will face criminal prosecution carrying prison terms of up to five years and fines of roughly $92,500.

[[FIG2]]

## Aligning With Washington and Trade Accords

The legislative push forms part of Taiwan's broader commitments under the Taiwan-U.S. Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, which the two governments signed on January 15, 2026. Under that bilateral pact, the United States lowered tariffs on the majority of Taiwanese goods from 20% to 15%. In exchange, Taiwanese companies pledged $250 billion in direct investments into American semiconductor manufacturing, clean energy, and AI infrastructure, supported by an additional $250 billion in credit guarantees.

Minister Kung noted that Taiwan's regulatory controls on sensitive items will increasingly mirror American export policies. The United States has enacted cascading export restrictions on advanced chips since 2022 to prevent sensitive computing hardware from aiding military modernization. Taiwan's shift to a blanket, market-wide restriction will match those standards by covering all prospective purchasers across China rather than tracking individual corporate rosters.

While Kung confirmed the regulatory direction, he did not provide a specific start date or final product list for the new regime, noting that the legislative process remains underway.

## Industry Impact Across Semiconductor Supply Chains

Closing the gray-market export conduit arrives during unprecedented expansion across Taiwan's domestic electronics manufacturing base. Semiconductor exports from Taiwan reached a record $87.2 billion in September 2026, marking a 60.9% increase compared to the same month in the prior year, according to trade data cited by [Trending Topics](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/taiwan-wants-to-make-a-i-chip-smuggling-to-china-a-crime/).

The enforcement shift brings distinct implications for major hardware providers operating across the region, as outlined by [24/7 Wall St.](https://247wallst.com/investing/2026/10/17/smuggling-nvidia-chips-into-china-is-about-to-become-a-crime-in-taiwan/). For chip designer Nvidia, which excluded China data center compute revenue from its fiscal third-quarter 2027 revenue outlook of $108.0 billion, halting gray-market channels through Taiwan carries minimal direct guidance risk while clarifying compliance boundaries. Meanwhile, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which recently lifted its fourth-quarter revenue guidance to $54.3 billion, operates primarily as a foundry fabricator rather than a systems exporter, insulating its core fabrication operations from server distribution liabilities.

Conversely, server assemblers that maintain manufacturing facilities in Taiwan face heightened compliance scrutiny. Super Micro Computer, whose board previously initiated an independent review into transactions connected to export control matters, remains exposed to transit enforcement. In July 2026, prosecutors investigated company executives on forgery charges, and in a separate U.S. investigation, a contractor linked to Super Micro pleaded guilty to diverting AI servers powered by Nvidia processors into China, according to Reuters reporting cited by [Taiwan News](https://taiwannews.com.tw/news/6459737).

As the draft legislation heads through Taiwan's parliament, trade officials and tech manufacturers will watch for the final statutory text to define licensing thresholds, compliance audits, and precise implementation timelines.

faq.q: What penalties will Taiwan impose for smuggling AI chips to China?
faq.a: Under the planned amendments to Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act, individuals caught smuggling controlled AI chips and servers will face criminal charges carrying up to five years in prison and fines of approximately $92,500.

faq.q: Why were prosecutors previously unable to file chip-smuggling criminal charges?
faq.a: Taiwan's prior export framework lacked specific statutory prohibitions covering advanced AI processors and servers. In past cases, such as an August 2026 scheme involving 130 diverted servers, prosecutors had to rely on indirect charges like document forgery and breach of trust.

faq.q: How does this move connect to trade agreements with the United States?
faq.a: The measures fulfill commitments under the Taiwan-U.S. Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed on January 15, 2026, which reduced U.S. tariffs on Taiwanese goods to 15% in exchange for technological alignment and $250 billion in Taiwanese corporate investments.
